passage: At the anganwadi, Parveen Miss put one coconut ladoo in front of each child. "If you wait until I come back from the kitchen, you get two." Imran stared at his ladoo. His hand crept toward it. Then he sat on both hands, hard. He turned his face to the window and started counting the crows on the wall. "One... two... four..." He hummed the morning rhyme, loudly. The girl beside him licked her ladoo, then ate it. Imran squeezed his eyes shut and kept humming. When Parveen Miss came back, he held up two fingers, grinning. "Two!"

qa.q: What did Imran count while he waited?
qa.a: He counted the crows on the wall.

qa.q: Why did Imran sit on his hands and turn to the window?
qa.a: Imran was tempted and restless, really wanting the ladoo, and keeping his hands and eyes busy helped him wait for two.

qa.q: What could Parveen Miss teach the other children from Imran's tricks?
qa.a: She could show them that looking away, humming or counting something makes waiting easier than staring at the sweet.

qa.q: How might the girl who ate her ladoo feel when Imran gets two?
qa.a: She may feel a little sad or jealous, having found it too hard to stop looking at the ladoo.

grounding: A small boy at the anganwadi sits on his hands and counts crows to wait for a second ladoo.

passage: I'm Sunaina, Nandini's aunt. On Sunday Nani put one gulab jamun on Nandini's plate and said, "If it's still there when I finish my prayer, you get another." I watched from the doorway. Nandini looked at it for a long time. Then she pushed the plate to the far end of the table and turned her chair to face the wall. She started telling her doll a story about a flying elephant. Once she peeked over her shoulder and quickly turned back. When Nani rang the little bell, Nandini spun round. The jamun was still there. I don't know what she was thinking, but she clapped like she'd won a race.

qa.q: What did Nani promise Nandini?
qa.a: If the gulab jamun was still there when Nani finished her prayer, Nandini would get another.

qa.q: Why did Nandini turn her chair to face the wall?
qa.a: She wanted the second jamun, and not seeing the sweet made it easier to wait.

qa.q: Which of Nandini's tricks could help another child wait?
qa.a: Moving the treat away and getting busy with a story, like telling a doll about a flying elephant, takes attention off the sweet.

qa.q: What might Nani feel when she sees the jamun still there?
qa.a: Nani may feel proud and amused that her granddaughter managed to wait, and happy to keep her promise 😊.

grounding: An aunt watches a small girl push away a sweet and tell her doll a story to wait for a second one.

passage:
Monday: Vidya's father, Raghav, set one toffee on the table. "Wait till I finish this call, and you get two." Vidya stared at it, touched it, sniffed it, and ate it in under a minute.
Wednesday: Appa tried again. This time he said, "Want to count the fan blades while you wait?" Vidya counted. Then she sat on her hands and sang her school song, very loudly. She peeked once. She kept singing. When Appa came back, the toffee was still there.
Saturday: Before Appa could say anything, Vidya put the toffee under a cup, turned her back and started building a block tower. "I'm busy," she told it. She got two.

qa.q: What did Vidya do with the toffee on Saturday?
qa.a: She put it under a cup, turned her back and started building a block tower.

qa.q: Why did Vidya sing her school song very loudly on Wednesday?
qa.a: Vidya felt impatient for the toffee, and singing loudly kept her mind off it, so it was easier to keep waiting for two.

qa.q: What change did Raghav make between Monday and Wednesday, and why did it help?
qa.a: He gave her something to do, counting the fan blades, which showed her that distraction makes waiting easier than staring.

qa.q: How might Raghav feel on Saturday when Vidya hides the toffee herself?
qa.a: He may feel proud and amused that she has learned the trick on her own.

grounding: Over a week, a small girl learns to hide the sweet and busy herself so she can wait for two.

passage: The wedding hall was loud and lunch was late. Manjula Aunty put one jalebi on Shreya's leaf. "If it's still there when I come back from greeting the bride, you get two." Shreya stared at the jalebi. Drums boomed, cousins ran past, and Aunty took a long time. Shreya sat on her hands. She turned her whole body toward the band and counted the drummers aloud, "One, two, three, four!" Then she counted balloons. When Manjula Aunty came back, the jalebi was still there, sticky from the heat. "Two!" Shreya shouted, holding up two fingers.

qa.q: What did Shreya count first while she waited?
qa.a: She counted the drummers aloud.

qa.q: Why did Shreya turn her whole body toward the band?
qa.a: She wanted the second jalebi, and not seeing the sweet made the wait easier; looking at the drummers kept her hands and mind busy.

qa.q: Which part of Shreya's waiting worked best, and why?
qa.a: Counting drummers and balloons; thinking about something else carried her through the long, noisy delay better than staring at the jalebi and trying hard.

qa.q: How might Manjula Aunty feel on coming back to the leaf?
qa.a: Manjula Aunty finds an untouched jalebi and a proud child holding up two fingers, and is likely delighted that Shreya waited so long in all that noise 😊

grounding: A young child sits on her hands and counts drummers to avoid eating a sweet so she can earn two.

passage: In the Kolkata flat, Vijay's mother, Sarita, put one sandesh on a steel plate. "I'm hanging the washing. Wait till I'm done and you get two." Vijay knelt by the table, nose almost touching the plate. He licked his lips. Then he pushed the plate behind the fruit bowl and ran to the window. "Tram!" he called. He sang the bus song twice, loudly, and hopped on one foot. When Sarita came back with the empty bucket, Vijay was on the floor making a train out of slippers. "Did you forget the sweet?" she asked. "No," he said. "I hid it from me."

qa.q: Where did Vijay push the plate?
qa.a: He pushed the plate behind the fruit bowl.

qa.q: What does 'I hid it from me' suggest about what Vijay was thinking?
qa.a: He knew that seeing the sandesh made waiting hard, so he wanted it out of sight and his mind on trams, songs and slippers.

qa.q: What could Sarita offer next time to make the wait easier from the start?
qa.a: She could suggest a song or a slipper train as soon as she sets the sweet down, and put the plate out of sight herself.

qa.q: How might Sarita feel hearing 'I hid it from me'?
qa.a: Sarita may be amused and quietly proud that her little boy found his own trick for waiting while she was busy with the washing.

grounding: A young child hides a sweet and busies himself with songs and play so he can earn a second one.
